titulo: How Scalping Works: Fast Trades, Risks, and Discipline
descricao: What the scalping strategy is, what tools and costs it requires, and why discipline matters more here than in other trading styles.
corpo:
Scalping is the name given to the strategy of opening many short trades throughout the day, seeking small profits on each one. Instead of waiting for a big price move, the scalper tries to capture smaller changes, over and over, closing each position within minutes — sometimes seconds.

It's a style that demands constant attention to the screen, quick reflexes in decision-making, and, above all, full control over operational costs, since the result of each individual trade tends to be small. This article explains how the method works in practice, what it demands from those who practice it, and in which situations it stops making sense.

The logic behind scalping

Instead of betting on a single trade with a distant target, the scalper adds up the result of dozens of smaller trades within the same session. If each successful trade yields, on average, R$ 8, and the trader manages to keep a favorable win rate across 30 trades in the day, the combined result can exceed that of a single, longer-breath trade — as long as the costs of each entry don't eat up a large part of that gain.

Why costs weigh more here than in other styles

Since each individual trade targets a small gain, the spread and brokerage fees represent a proportionally larger slice of the result. A R$ 0.50 spread on a R$ 5 profit target already eats up 10% of the potential gain before the trade even starts moving in its favor. Because of that, scalpers tend to prioritize assets with higher liquidity and more competitive spreads, and avoid trading during low-volume hours, when that cost tends to rise.

Tools that help with this style

  • Short-timeframe charts, like 1 minute or 5 minutes, to follow price action in real time.
  • Fast-responding momentum indicators, to identify entries and exits quickly.
  • A plan of daily profit targets and maximum loss, set before the session starts.
  • A simple routine for logging trades, since the high volume of entries makes it easy to lose track of how many trades have already been made that day.

An example of risk management for the day

Imagine a trader with R$ 2,000 allocated to this strategy, willing to risk 0.5% per trade — R$ 10. If the goal is to make between 15 and 25 trades in the day, a daily loss limit equal to 3% of capital (R$ 60) prevents a bad streak in the morning from compromising the rest of the session. Upon hitting that limit, the trader ends the day, regardless of how much time remains until the market closes — the discipline to stop matters just as much as the entry strategy itself.

Advantages and limitations of scalping

Among the advantages is lower exposure to long-term events, since positions stay open for a short time, reducing the risk of being caught off guard by overnight news. On the other hand, the method demands intense screen time, fast decisions under pressure, and a higher tolerance for losing trades, since not every attempt to capture a small move works out — which also weighs on the trader's emotional side.

Who it makes sense for

Scalping tends to work best for those who can dedicate uninterrupted blocks of attention to the market, have the tolerance to handle a string of small losses without changing the plan, and trade assets liquid enough to keep costs under control. Those who prefer to decide calmly and check the market only a few times a day will probably get frustrated with this pace, and tend to do better with longer time frames.

Scalping isn't synonymous with trading faster at any cost

A common mistake among people trying this style for the first time is confusing trade volume with decision quality. Opening a new position just because a minute has gone by with no entry, without a clear technical signal, tends to produce worse results than patiently waiting for the next opportunity within the criteria set out in the plan. Well-executed scalping still follows rules — just within a shorter time window than other styles, and with less tolerance for straying from the original plan.

Before applying scalping with real capital, it's worth simulating the strategy for a few weeks, timing the effort involved, counting the costs of each trade, and checking whether the net result, after deducting spread and brokerage, really justifies the effort and wear involved.
